claim: The CNN classifier achieved 92-96% accuracy for freezing behavior classification across different experimental chambers and neural headgears.
source: Each classifier achieved optimal training within 50 training epochs (Figure 1—figure supplement 1B–E) and yielded 92–96% accuracy, 5–10% false positive rate (FPR) and 4–6% false negative rate (FNR) (Figure 1D).
evidence: The manuscript reports specific accuracy percentages from CNN performance testing across different conditions.

claim: The CNN classifier performance was comparable to the relative performance between two human observers.
source: This was comparable to the relative performance between two humans: given one person's scoring held as ground truth, the other person scored with 95% accuracy, 11.5% FPR and 0.3% FNR (Figure 1—figure supplement 1F).
evidence: Direct comparison of CNN metrics to human observer metrics is provided.

claim: The CNN better reflected human observer scoring than FreezeFrame software.
source: We found that the CNN better reflected the human observer than FreezeFrame (Figure 1E). The CNN and human observer yielded a correlation of 0.96 (Pearson correlation, Figure 1F), while FreezeFrame and human observer yielded a correlation of 0.85 (Pearson correlation, Figure 1G).
evidence: Correlation coefficients comparing CNN and FreezeFrame to human observers are provided.

claim: Mice froze very little during habituation, quickly increased freezing during conditioning, and slowly decreased freezing over three days of extinction.
source: Mice froze very little during habituation, quickly increased freezing during conditioning, and slowly decreased freezing to the tone over three days of extinction (Figure 2B).
evidence: Behavioral data across experimental conditions is described and referenced in Figure 2B.

claim: During fear extinction, a neural correlate of RPE should have suppressed activity during a tone paired with footshock and elevated activity at tone offset when shock is omitted.
source: During fear extinction, we expect a neural correlate of RPE to have suppressed activity during a tone that has been paired with a foot shock to signal worse than expected outcome, and elevated activity during the tone offset to signal better than expected outcome because the footshock was omitted.
evidence: This is a theoretical prediction based on RPE theory applied to fear extinction.

claim: A neural correlate of salience can be considered an unsigned prediction error, or the absolute value of RPE.
source: A neural correlate of salience, which can be considered an unsigned prediction error, or the absolute value of RPE, should instead have elevated activity during the tone that has been paired with a footshock, and elevated activity at the tone offset, when the shock was unexpectedly omitted (Figure 2C).
evidence: This defines salience in relation to RPE based on established theoretical frameworks.

claim: Both medial and lateral VTA showed increased activity to reward.
source: We found that both regions showed increased activity to reward (Figure 3—figure supplement 2).
evidence: Fiber photometry recordings during reward consumption are referenced.

claim: During habituation and fear conditioning, medial and lateral VTA DA neuron signals were similar.
source: During habituation and fear conditioning, medial and lateral VTA DA neuron signals were similar, but could not be easily explained as purely RPE or salience (Figure 3—figure supplement 1D,E top two rows, and F-H).
evidence: Comparison of neural activity patterns across VTA subregions during specific behavioral phases.

claim: GCaMP6f fluorescence in both medial and lateral VTA decreased throughout the tone during habituation and conditioning.
source: GCaMP6f fluorescence in both regions decreased throughout the tone during habituation and conditioning.
evidence: Direct observation from fiber photometry recordings.

claim: Both medial and lateral VTA showed increased fluorescence to the shock.
source: Both regions also showed increased fluorescence to the shock (Figure 3—figure supplement 1B,C).
evidence: Fiber photometry data during shock presentation.

claim: During fear extinction, medial VTA DA neuron activity was consistent with RPE.
source: Medial VTA DA neuron activity was consistent with RPE (Figure 2C): GCAMP6f fluorescence decreased throughout the tone that had been associated with a negative outcome, and increased at the offset of the tone, during the omission of the expected shock (Figure 3E; percentile rank of the mean GCaMP6f fluorescence every second relative to shuffled data: p<0.01 after Bonferroni correction for multiple time point comparison).
evidence: Statistical analysis of fiber photometry data showing activity patterns consistent with RPE predictions.

claim: Both RPE-like signals in medial VTA diminished in magnitude throughout extinction.
source: Both of these signals diminished in magnitude throughout extinction, as expected with RPE.
evidence: Observation of signal changes across extinction days consistent with RPE theory.

claim: During fear extinction, lateral VTA DA neuron activity was more consistent with salience.
source: In contrast, during fear extinction, lateral VTA DA neuron activity was more consistent with salience (Figure 2C). GCaMP6f fluorescence increased at the tone onset, consistent with an unsigned prediction error (Figure 3F; percentile rank of the mean GCaMP6f fluorescence every second relative to shuffled data: p<0.01 after Bonferroni correction for multiple time point comparisons).
evidence: Statistical analysis of fiber photometry data showing activity patterns consistent with salience predictions.

claim: GCaMP6f fluorescence in lateral VTA increased at tone offset, consistent with the omission of shock being salient.
source: GCaMP6f fluorescence also increased at the tone offset, consistent with the idea that the omission of the shock is salient.
evidence: Fiber photometry data interpreted in the context of salience theory.

claim: Both salience-like signals in lateral VTA diminished throughout extinction as the tone loses its salience.
source: Both these signals also diminished throughout extinction, as the tone loses its salience.
evidence: Observation of signal changes across extinction days interpreted through salience framework.

claim: SNc DA neurons showed different activity profiles from lateral VTA during fear extinction.
source: To control for the possibility that the lateral VTA signal could be coming from the adjacent SNc, in a separate group of mice we recorded from SNc and found different activity profiles (Figure 3—figure supplement 3).
evidence: Control experiment with fiber photometry recordings from SNc.

claim: Control mice expressing GFP or YFP showed little modulation in fluorescence signal except at the time of shock.
source: There was little modulation in the signal in the control mice. The exception was the time of the shock, which generated depressed fluorescence, which was the opposite of the increased fluorescence observed with GCaMP6f in medial and lateral VTA (Figure 3—figure supplement 4).
evidence: Control experiment data showing minimal signal in non-calcium indicator conditions.

claim: Dopamine axons in the nucleus accumbens and DMS both showed RPE during fear extinction, similar to dopamine cell bodies in medial VTA.
source: We found that dopamine axons in the nucleus accumbens and DMS both showed RPE during fear extinction, similar to dopamine cell bodies in medial VTA (Figure 3—figure supplement 5).
evidence: Fiber photometry recordings from DA axons in striatal regions.

claim: In medial VTA, there was a negative correlation between freezing during the tone and GCaMP6f fluorescence during tone onset on a trial-by-trial basis.
source: In the medial VTA DA neurons, we observed a negative correlation between freezing during the tone and GCaMP6f fluorescence during the tone onset of the same trial (Figure 4A; one sample t-test p=0.021, n = 10 mice)
evidence: Statistical analysis of trial-by-trial correlations between behavior and neural activity.

claim: In medial VTA, there was a positive correlation between freezing during the tone and GCaMP6f fluorescence at tone offset on a trial-by-trial basis.
source: but a positive correlation between freezing during the tone and GCaMP6f fluorescence at the tone offset of the same trial (Figure 4A; one sample t-test p<10−4, n = 10 mice).
evidence: Statistical analysis of trial-by-trial correlations between behavior and neural activity.

claim: The negative correlation between medial VTA fluorescence during tone and freezing reflects the learned negative association with the tone.
source: Specifically, the negative correlation between fluorescence during the tone and freezing is consistent with the idea that the degree of inhibition in DA during the tone reflects the learned negative association with the tone (Mileykovskiy and Morales, 2011).
evidence: Interpretation of correlation data in the context of prior literature on DA and aversive learning.

claim: The positive correlation between medial VTA DA after tone and freezing reflects the degree of 'relief' when expected shock is omitted.
source: Similarly, the positive correlation between DA after the tone and freezing is consistent with the idea that the fluorescence reflects the degree of 'relief' that the animal experiences when the expected shock is omitted.
evidence: Interpretation of correlation data in the context of RPE theory.

claim: Mice with lower average medial VTA GCaMP6f fluorescence during tone onset froze more to the tone across animals.
source: Mice with lower average GCaMP6f fluorescence during the tone onset or higher average GCaMP6f fluorescence at the tone offset froze more to the tone (Pearson's correlation between GCaMP6f 5 s after tone onset and freezing during tone: r = −0.644, p=0.044
evidence: Cross-animal correlation analysis between neural activity and behavior.

claim: Mice with higher average medial VTA GCaMP6f fluorescence at tone offset froze more to the tone across animals.
source: Mice with lower average GCaMP6f fluorescence during the tone onset or higher average GCaMP6f fluorescence at the tone offset froze more to the tone (Pearson's correlation between GCaMP6f 5 s after tone onset and freezing during tone: r = −0.644, p=0.044; GCaMP6f 5 s after tone offset and freezing during tone: r = 0.768, p=0.010).
evidence: Cross-animal correlation analysis between neural activity and behavior.

claim: In lateral VTA, there was a positive correlation across trials between freezing throughout the tone and GCaMP6f during tone onset.
source: In contrast, in the lateral VTA, we observed a positive correlation across trials between freezing throughout the tone and GCaMP6f during the tone onset for each trial (Figure 4D; one sample t-test p<10−4, n = 11 mice)
evidence: Statistical analysis of trial-by-trial correlations between behavior and neural activity.

claim: In lateral VTA, there was no significant correlation between freezing and GCaMP6f at tone offset on a trial-by-trial basis.
source: but not the tone offset (Figure 4D; one sample t-test p=0.071).
evidence: Statistical analysis showing lack of significant correlation.

claim: The positive correlation between lateral VTA fluorescence during tone onset and freezing reflects that more salient stimuli elicit more freezing.
source: This is consistent with the interpretation that fluorescence during the tone in lateral VTA reflects the salience of the tone, given that more salient stimuli should elicit more freezing.
evidence: Interpretation of correlation data in the context of salience theory.

claim: NpHR-mediated photoinhibition produced peak photocurrents of 332.15 ± 64.79 pA during voltage clamp recordings.
source: Left: Mean and SEM of photocurrents evoked during voltage clamp (n = 7 neurons; peak current: 332.15 ± 64.79 pA; steady state current: 318.84 ± 63.64 pA).
evidence: Ex vivo electrophysiology measurements of optogenetic inhibition efficacy.

claim: NpHR-mediated hyperpolarization during current clamp showed peak hyperpolarization of 92.76 ± 14.58 mV from baseline.
source: Mean and SEM of NpHR-mediated hyperpolarization during current clamp (n = 7 neurons; peak hyperpolarization from baseline: 92.76 ± 14.58 mV; steady state hyperpolarization from baseline: 62.93 ± 10.92 mV).
evidence: Ex vivo electrophysiology measurements of optogenetic inhibition efficacy.

claim: Inhibiting either medial or lateral VTA DA caused real time place aversion to the inhibition chamber.
source: Inhibiting either medial or lateral VTA DA caused real time place aversion to the inhibition chamber (Figure 5—figure supplement 1D; 2-factor ANOVA with group and subregion as factors: group effect: F(1,1) = 103.33, p = 10−14; subregion effect: F(1,1) = 0.32, p = 0.576; group × subregion interaction: F(1,1) = 0.01, p = 0.935)
evidence: Behavioral data from real-time place aversion assay with statistical analysis.

claim: Inhibiting either medial or lateral VTA DA decreased velocity during inhibition.
source: and decreased velocity during inhibition (Figure 5—figure supplement 1E; 2-factor ANOVA with group and subregion as factors: group effect: F(1,1) = 14.35, p < 10−3; subregion effect: F(1,1) = 0.1, p = 0.754; group × subregion interaction: F(1,1) = 0, p = 0.9441).
evidence: Behavioral data from real-time place aversion assay with statistical analysis.

claim: Inhibiting medial VTA DA neurons at tone offset caused NpHR mice to freeze more to the tone compared to YFP controls.
source: Inhibiting medial VTA DA neurons at tone offset yielded an effect consistent with the representation of RPE in this subregion: NpHR mice froze more to the tone compared to the YFP controls (Figure 5F-H; 2-factor ANOVA with group and tone number as factors, tone number being a repeated measure: group effect: F(1,62) = 7.528, p = 0.012; group × tone number interaction: F(1,62) = 1.056 p = 0.361).
evidence: Optogenetic manipulation experiment with behavioral readout and statistical analysis.

claim: Medial VTA NpHR mice increased freezing during the inhibition period compared to YFP controls.
source: In addition to attenuating extinction of tone-induced freezing, NpHR mice increased freezing during and after the inhibition period compared to YFP controls (2-factor ANOVA with group and tone number as factors, tone number being a repeated measure. During 6 s inhibition period: group effect: F(1,62) = 17.668, p < 10−3; group × tone number interaction: F(1,62) = 1.371 p = 0.032.
evidence: Optogenetic manipulation experiment with behavioral readout and statistical analysis.

claim: Medial VTA NpHR mice increased freezing after the inhibition period compared to YFP controls.
source: During 6 s after inhibition period: group effect: F(1,62) = 28.082, p < 10−4; group × tone number interaction: F(1,62) = 0.854 p = 0.782.)
evidence: Optogenetic manipulation experiment with behavioral readout and statistical analysis.

claim: Medial VTA DA neurons lead to updating of the value (or freezing behavior) upon subsequent presentations of the tone that preceded inhibition.
source: Thus, not only do medial VTA DA neurons lead to updating of the value (or freezing behavior) upon subsequent presentations of the tone that preceded inhibition, they also modify behavior subsequent to the inhibition period.
evidence: Interpretation of optogenetic manipulation results in the context of learning theory.

claim: Inhibiting lateral VTA DA neurons at tone offset yielded no change in freezing during the tone.
source: In contrast to the effects observed with medial VTA inhibition, inhibiting the lateral VTA DA neurons at tone offset yielded no change in freezing during the tone (Figure 5I-K; 2-factor ANOVA with group and tone number as factors, tone number being a repeated measure: group effect: F(1,62) = 0.002, p = 0.964; group × tone number interaction: F(1,62) = 1.121 p = 0.249).
evidence: Optogenetic manipulation experiment with behavioral readout and statistical analysis.

claim: Lateral VTA tone offset inhibition increased freezing after the inhibition period, an effect that increased with extinction.
source: This manipulation did, however, increase freezing after the inhibition period, an effect that increased with extinction (2-factor ANOVA with group and tone number as factors, tone number being a repeated measure: group effect: F(1,62) = 6.981, p = 0.019; group × tone number interaction: F(1,62) = 1.480 p = 0.011).
evidence: Optogenetic manipulation experiment with behavioral readout and statistical analysis.

claim: Lateral VTA inhibition primarily affects freezing at time points after inhibition, rather than causing learned changes in the value of preceding events.
source: This suggests that lateral VTA inhibition primarily affects freezing at time points after inhibition, rather than causing learned changes in the value of preceding events.
evidence: Interpretation of optogenetic manipulation results comparing temporal effects.

claim: Inhibiting SNc DA neurons at tone offset did not have an effect on tone freezing.
source: Similar to the lateral VTA cohort, inhibiting SNc DA neurons at tone offset did not have an effect on tone freezing.
evidence: Optogenetic manipulation experiment in control region.

claim: SNc NpHR mice showed decreased freezing during the ITI relative to the YFP group.
source: However, SNc NpHR mice showed decreased freezing during the ITI relative to the YFP group (Figure 5—figure supplement 3D; 2-factor ANOVA with group and tone number as factors, tone number being a repeated measure: group effect: F(1,62) = 4.980, p = 0.047; group × tone interaction: F(1,62) = 1.276, p 0.081)
evidence: Optogenetic manipulation experiment in control region with statistical analysis.

claim: Lateral VTA and SNc inhibition during cue offset may not have identical consequences.
source: This suggests that lateral VTA and SNc inhibition during the cue offset may not have identical consequences.
evidence: Comparison of optogenetic manipulation effects across regions.

claim: Inhibiting lateral VTA DA neurons at tone onset caused NpHR mice to extinguish more slowly to the tone.
source: We found that NpHR mice extinguished more slowly to the tone. This is reflected in that there was no main effect of group, but a significant interaction between group and tone number (Figure 6C, D; 2-factor ANOVA with group and tone number as factors, tone number being a repeated measure: group effect: F(1,62) = 0.014, p = 0.908; group × tone number interaction: F(1,62) = 2.217, p < 10−6).
evidence: Optogenetic manipulation experiment with behavioral readout and statistical analysis.

claim: Lateral VTA tone onset NpHR mice showed decreased freezing during the ITI.
source: Additionally, we observed that NpHR mice showed decreased freezing during the ITI (Figure 6D; 2-factor ANOVA with group and tone number as factors, tone number being a repeated measure: group effect: F(1,62) = 6.477, p = 0.019; group × tone number interaction: F(1,62) = 1.562 p = 0.004).
evidence: Optogenetic manipulation experiment with behavioral readout and statistical analysis.

claim: Inhibiting the salience-like signal at tone onset slows extinction learning over time.
source: Together with the results from the previous experiments, this suggests that inhibiting the salience-like signal at tone onset slows extinction learning over time, even though activity of these neurons at tone offset does not update the value of the preceding tone.
evidence: Synthesis of optogenetic manipulation results across different timing conditions.

claim: During fear extinction, medial VTA more closely resembled RPE, while lateral VTA more closely resembled salience.
source: Here, we found that during fear extinction, medial VTA more closely resembled RPE, while lateral VTA more closely resembled salience.
evidence: Summary statement integrating fiber photometry findings.

claim: Activity in both medial and lateral VTA subregions contributed causally to fear extinction, but the temporal relationship between activity and freezing differed.
source: While activity in both subregions contributed causally to fear extinction, the temporal relationship between activity and freezing differed.
evidence: Summary statement integrating optogenetic manipulation findings.

claim: Inhibition in medial VTA prevented the update of value to the tone preceding the inhibition, causing freezing to be more likely on subsequent tone presentations.
source: Consistent with the idea that RPE signals update the value of preceding events, inhibition in medial VTA prevented the update of value (or freezing response) to the tone preceding the inhibition, causing freezing to be more likely on subsequent tone presentations.
evidence: Interpretation of medial VTA optogenetic results in the context of RPE theory.

claim: Inhibition of the salience-like signal in lateral VTA affected freezing during or immediately following inhibition, but did not update the value to subsequent presentations of the tone if it preceded the inhibition.
source: In contrast, inhibition of the salience-like signal in lateral VTA affected freezing in the time period during or immediately following the inhibition, but did not update the value (or freezing response) to subsequent presentations of the tone if it preceded the inhibition.
evidence: Interpretation of lateral VTA optogenetic results in the context of salience theory.

claim: VTA DA neurons are known to be modulated by aversive stimuli and have been implicated in fear conditioning and extinction.
source: DA neurons originating in the VTA are known to be modulated by aversive stimuli, and have been implicated in fear conditioning and extinction (El-Ghundi et al., 2001; Young et al., 1993; Inoue et al., 2000; Nader and LeDoux, 1999; Guarraci and Kapp, 1999; Holtzman-Assif et al., 2010; Delgado et al., 2008; Luo et al., 2018; Salinas-Hernández et al., 2018; Zweifel et al., 2011; Pezze and Feldon, 2004; Mueller et al., 2010; Pignatelli et al., 2017; Nasehi et al., 2016; Pezze et al., 2003; Budygin et al., 2012; Robinson et al., 2019; Lammel et al., 2011; Jo et al., 2018; Lutas et al., 2019; Fadok et al., 2009; Groessl et al., 2018; Bouchet et al., 2018; Wenzel et al., 2018; Wang and Tsien, 2011; Mileykovskiy and Morales, 2011).
evidence: Summary of prior literature with extensive citations.

claim: A critical function of VTA DA neurons is to signal reward prediction error (RPE).
source: A critical function of VTA DA neurons is to signal reward prediction error (RPE), or the difference between experienced and expected reward (Schultz et al., 1997; Cohen et al., 2012).
evidence: Statement of established theory with citations.

claim: RPE signals support reinforcement learning.
source: This signal supports reinforcement learning (Steinberg et al., 2013; Chang et al., 2016; Tsai et al., 2009; Witten et al., 2011; Parker et al., 2016; Saunders et al., 2018; Zweifel et al., 2009; Kim et al., 2012; Stopper et al., 2014; Adamantidis et al., 2011).
evidence: Statement of established theory with citations.

claim: VTA DA neurons can display heterogeneous and spatially organized signals rather than uniformly representing a scalar RPE.
source: However, rather than uniformly representing a scalar RPE, there is recent appreciation that VTA DA neurons can display heterogeneous and spatially organized signals.
evidence: Summary of recent findings in the field.

claim: During navigation-based decision making, there are spatially segregated representations within VTA DA neurons of sensory, motor, and cognitive variables.
source: For example, we recently demonstrated that during navigation-based decision making, there are spatially segregated representations within VTA DA neurons of a variety of sensory, motor, and cognitive variables (Engelhard et al., 2019).
evidence: Reference to prior work by the authors.

claim: Neural correlates of salience-like signals have been demonstrated in certain DA neurons.
source: Others have demonstrated neural correlates of salience-like signals in certain DA neurons (de Jong et al., 2019; Saddoris et al., 2015; Wang and Tsien, 2011; Gore et al., 2014; Yuan et al., 2019; Cho et al., 2017; Aitken et al., 2016).
evidence: Summary of prior literature with citations.

claim: VTA DA neurons were shown to represent RPE-like signals during fear extinction, displaying elevated activity when shock is omitted at cue offset.
source: In particular, VTA DA neurons were shown to represent RPE-like signals during fear extinction, in that they display elevated activity when the shock is omitted at the offset of the cue, signaling better-than-expected outcome (Salinas-Hernández et al., 2018; Badrinarayan et al., 2012; Jo et al., 2018).
evidence: Summary of prior literature with citations.

claim: Manipulation of RPE-like activity in DA neurons altered the rate of extinction, suggesting this signal drives reinforcement learning for aversive associations.
source: Manipulation of this activity altered the rate of extinction, suggesting that an RPE-like signal in DA neurons drives reinforcement learning for aversive associations as well as rewarding associations (Salinas-Hernández et al., 2018; Luo et al., 2018).
evidence: Summary of prior literature with citations.

claim: Freezing traditionally requires hand scoring when mice are tethered to neural headgear, as existing software cannot dissociate tether movement from mouse movement.
source: However, one limitation of freezing as a readout of learning is that it traditionally requires hand scoring when mice are tethered to neural headgear, as existing software is not designed to dissociate tether movement from mouse movement (Luyten et al., 2014; Shoji et al., 2014).
evidence: Statement of technical limitation with citations.

claim: The CNN was initialized on the pre-trained ResNet18 architecture.
source: The CNN was initialized on the pre-trained ResNet18 architecture (He et al., 2016), and further trained on 'difference images,' the pixel-by-pixel intensity difference between consecutive pairs of frames.
evidence: Description of computational methods with citation.

claim: The rationale for inputting difference images to the CNN was to capture frame-by-frame motion.
source: The rationale for inputting difference images to the CNN was to capture frame-by-frame motion.
evidence: Explanation of methodological design choice.

claim: The correlation between two human observers was 0.98 (Pearson correlation).
source: In comparison, the correlation between two human observers was 0.98 (Pearson correlation, Figure 1—figure supplement 1F).
evidence: Benchmark data for human performance.

claim: The CNN pipeline analyzed over 500 hrs of behavioral data during fear conditioning and extinction.
source: In this paper, we used the CNN to analyze over 500 hrs of behavioral data during fear conditioning and extinction, which would have been prohibitively time consuming without an automated approach.
evidence: Description of the scale of data analysis performed.

claim: There is electrophysiological, anatomical and functional evidence for a medial/lateral distinction within the VTA.
source: We chose these subregions because of the electrophysiological, anatomical and functional evidence that there is a medial/lateral distinction within the VTA (Lammel et al., 2014; Beier et al., 2015; Yang et al., 2018; Engelhard et al., 2019; de Jong et al., 2019).
evidence: Justification for experimental design based on prior literature.

claim: The SNc has a greater proportion of DA neurons that signal salience rather than RPE compared to VTA.
source: Specifically, there is previous evidence that the SNc, which is lateral to the VTA, has a greater proportion of DA neurons that signal salience rather than RPE (Matsumoto and Hikosaka, 2009; Menegas et al., 2017).
evidence: Summary of prior literature with citations.

claim: An animal's speed may be a reflection of the motivational salience of an environment.
source: One possible relationship between these seemingly disconnected findings of salience versus kinematic tuning is that an animal's speed is a reflection of the motivational salience of an environment (Zenon et al., 2016; Panigrahi et al., 2015; Wang et al., 2013).
evidence: Speculative interpretation linking different findings with citations.

claim: The medial/lateral distinction between RPE and salience does not hold across all behaviors.
source: It is worth noting that this medial/lateral distinction between RPE and salience does not hold across all behaviors (Heymann et al., 2020).
evidence: Acknowledgment of limitations with citation.

claim: During fear conditioning, medial and lateral VTA shared similar activity profiles, which may reflect heterogeneity in single neuron activity not captured with fiber photometry.
source: In fact, we found that during fear conditioning, medial and lateral VTA shared similar activity profiles, which may reflect heterogeneity in single neuron activity that is not captured with fiber photometry.
evidence: Interpretation of findings acknowledging methodological limitations.

claim: Inhibition of a subpopulation of VTA neurons with projections to NAc Core did not affect extinction.
source: This was consistent with the previous observation that inhibition of a subpopulation of VTA neurons with projections to NAc Core did not affect extinction (Luo et al., 2018).
evidence: Comparison with prior literature with citation.

claim: Despite differences in neural correlates, different VTA/SNc DA subpopulations share a common function of mediating learning.
source: This is consistent with the emerging framework that despite differences in neural correlates, different VTA/SNc DA subpopulations share a common function of mediating learning, even though they may differ in the specific setting in which they contribute to learning, or the specific aspect of learning that they mediate (Ellwood et al., 2017; Saunders et al., 2018; Cox and Witten, 2019; Bromberg-Martin et al., 2010; Menegas et al., 2018).
evidence: Synthesis of findings in the context of broader theoretical framework with citations.

claim: Dat-Cre mice were crossed with Ai148D mice to express GCaMP6f in DA neurons for fiber photometry recordings.
source: To perform fiber photometry recordings from VTA DA neurons, we expressed the calcium indicator GCaMP6f in DA neurons by crossing Dat-Cre mice with Ai148D mice (see Materials and methods; Engelhard et al., 2019).
evidence: Description of experimental methods.

claim: Optic fibers were targeted to either medial VTA (n=10 mice) or lateral VTA (n=11 mice) for fiber photometry recordings.
source: We targeted the recording fiber to either medial or lateral VTA (Figure 3A–C, Figure 3—figure supplement 1A; medial VTA group: n = 10 mice, lateral VTA group: n = 11 mice).
evidence: Description of experimental design and sample sizes.

claim: Mice were group housed with up to five other mice and allowed ad libitum access to food and water.
source: Mice were group housed with up to five other mice, allowed ad libitum access to food and water, and kept on a 12 hr light on and 12 hr light-off schedule.
evidence: Description of animal husbandry conditions.

claim: Mice between 7-10 weeks of age were used during surgery.
source: Mice between 7–10 weeks of age were used during surgery.
evidence: Description of experimental subjects.

claim: All experiments followed guidelines established by the National Institutes of Health and were reviewed by Princeton University IACUC.
source: All experiments followed guidelines established by the National Institutes of Health and reviewed by Princeton University Institutional Animals Care and Use Committee (IACUC).
evidence: Statement of ethical compliance.
